question: What is the main goal of using aseptic technique in the ward?

options.A: To prevent pathogen contamination during clinical procedures
options.B: To cure patients who already have active bacterial infections
options.C: To completely eliminate all microbes from the hospital environment
options.D: To reduce the financial cost of hospital-acquired illnesses

explanation: You've got this! Aseptic techniques are just safe practices we use to stop harmful germs from getting into clean or sterile parts of the body during procedures. Keep it up! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why is infection control a team duty for all healthcare workers?

options.A: Because cleaning supplies are distributed equally among departments
options.B: Because a single mistake by any staff member can put a patient at risk
options.C: Because only doctors are allowed to handle sterile equipment
options.D: Because hospital management requires daily written reports from nurses

explanation: Spot on! Keeping patients safe is a team effort. Because we all work together around the patient, one small slip by anyone can let germs spread—so every member's vigilance counts. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h1)

question: Which of these everyday nursing actions is an example of medical asepsis?

options.A: Performing an open surgical operation in the theatre
options.B: Wiping down a bedside table with a disinfectant wipe
options.C: Putting on sterile surgical gloves and a gown
options.D: Inserting a urinary catheter using a sterile kit

explanation: Great job! Medical asepsis is all about clean habits—like wiping down surfaces to cut down on germs. Surgical asepsis is what we save for deep, sterile procedures. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h2)

question: When should you as a nurse switch to surgical asepsis instead of medical asepsis?

options.A: Before giving oral medication to a patient in the general ward
options.B: During any procedure that enters a normally sterile body cavity
options.C: After finishing a routine bed bath for an adult patient
options.D: Whenever entering a patient room with a known respiratory infection

explanation: You're doing great! Whenever we do invasive things like passing a catheter or assisting in theater, we need total sterility to protect deep body tissues from infection. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h2)

question: What should you do if you are unsure whether a sterile package is still clean?

options.A: Use the item quickly before anyone notices the error
options.B: Treat the item as contaminated and get a new one
options.C: Ask another nurse to guess if the item is still safe
options.D: Wipe the outside package with alcohol and use it anyway

explanation: Safety first! In nursing, if there is ever any doubt about an item's sterility, we assume it's contaminated and grab a fresh one. Never gamble with a patient's safety. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h3)

question: Why is the outer one-inch border of a sterile field considered unsterile?

options.A: Because nurses are only allowed to touch the exact center of the tray
options.B: Because air currents move faster along the edges of a paper wrap
options.C: Because the manufacturer marks that area with special invisible ink
options.D: Because it is likely to touch unsterile surfaces during setup and handling

explanation: Makes sense, right? That outer edge is bound to brush against your hands or the table surface while you open it, so we treat it as a safe buffer zone that's no longer sterile. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h3)

question: What is the single most effective way to stop the spread of infections in the hospital?
explanation: Simple yet powerful! Washing or sanitizing your hands properly is your number one shield against carrying germs from patient to patient. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h4)

question: You just removed a dirty dressing from a draining wound while wearing gloves. What is your immediate next step after taking them off?

options.A: Put on a fresh pair of clean gloves
options.B: Touch the clean patient chart safely
options.D: Write the nursing notes in the chart

explanation: Always clean your hands right after taking off gloves! Microbes can easily slip through tiny, unseen tears in gloves, so hand hygiene seals the deal. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h4)

question: When opening a wrapped sterile package on your tray, which flap should you open first?

options.A: The left side flap of the paper wrap
options.B: The right side flap of the paper wrap
options.C: The flap furthest away from the body
options.D: The flap closest to the nurse's chest

explanation: You've got this! Opening the far flap first means your hands won't have to reach directly across the clean items you just exposed. Smart and safe! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h5)

question: Why must you never leave a set-up sterile field unattended on the ward?

options.A: Because sterile drapes automatically fold up after five minutes
options.B: Because the sterile items will melt if exposed to room air
options.C: Because someone might contaminate it without your knowledge
options.D: Because hospital regulations fine nurses who walk away from trays

explanation: Spot on! If you walk away, someone might unknowingly brush against it or contaminate it, ruining your sterile setup. Stay close to your work! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h5)

question: Which of these hospital items is considered critical and needs full sterilization?
explanation: Brilliant! Scalpels cut deep into sterile body tissues, so they must be 100% free of all germs and spores through proper sterilization. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h6)

question: What is the main difference between disinfection and sterilization?

options.A: Sterilization is only used on patient skin, while disinfection is used on metal tools
options.B: Disinfection uses high-pressure steam, while sterilization uses simple soap and water
options.C: Sterilization destroys all microorganisms and spores, while disinfection reduces their numbers
options.D: Disinfection kills bacterial spores, while sterilization only kills active living fungi

explanation: Think of it this way: sterilization wipes out *everything* including tough spores, while disinfection just lowers the germ count on surfaces to a safe level. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h6)

question: What do we mean by a healthcare-associated infection (HAI)?

options.A: An infectious disease that doctors catch from patients in the clinic
options.B: An infection acquired by a patient while receiving treatment in a hospital
options.C: A chronic illness that people inherit from their parents at birth
options.D: A skin rash caused by wearing dirty uniforms outside the ward

explanation: You're doing awesome! An HAI is simply an infection a patient picks up while receiving care in the hospital—something they didn't have when they first checked in. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h7)

question: Which of these actions is NOT a way nurses help prevent healthcare-associated infections?

options.A: Prescribing strong antibiotic medications to every new patient
options.B: Changing surgical wound dressings according to hospital policy
options.C: Using sterile technique during invasive urinary catheter insertions
options.D: Practicing consistent hand hygiene before and after patient contact

explanation: Spot on! Nurses don't prescribe drugs, and giving antibiotics to everyone would cause dangerous drug resistance rather than stop infections. Good catch! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T2#GNS122_U2_T2_h7)
